newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: SIMEX plans launch of revised gas oil futures.
newsitem.headline: SIMEX plans launch of revised gas oil futures.

text.p: The Singapore International Monetary Exchange in Singapore (SIMEX) is planning to launch a revised gas oil contract, industry sources said on Wednesday.
They said a senior SIMEX official and 12 traders met on Wednesday and decided to develop a futures contract with physical delivery rather than cash settlement.
They said planning was at an early stage and pecifications for the contract had not been discussed.
"This is just our first meeting and it is too premature to talk about specifications," said one trader.
SIMEX officials declined to comment.
SIMEX launched a gas oil futures contract in 1991 but it was delisted in 1993 as traders withdrew their support for trading the contract.
The SIMEX plans will clash with those of the New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX), which is planning both a gas oil futures and crude futures contract for Asia.
NYMEX operates a screen-based trading system called ACCESS outside NYMEX floor trading hours.

A meeting of the Asia-Pacific Advisory Committee, formed last year to develop NYMEX energy products for Asia, recommended earlier this year that NYMEX should pursue a gas oil futures contract, also based on physical delivery.
NYMEX plans to survey traders to help define contract terms and specifications, trade sources said.
The push to develop contracts for Asia could dramatically change the energy trading landscape, market sources said.

Asia is expected to be the world's biggest consumer of energy by 2000, surpassing North America. Nevertheless, traders said Asia had little say in determining global pricing because of its lack of a successful futures market.
Most trading of hedge instruments is carried out over the counter (OTC).
Futures trading would give prices more visibility in Asia and start to influence global prices, some market participants said.
NYMEX is also considering a futures contract on a basket of crudes to be settled in cash.

But Asia's ability to determine crude prices will remain limited as the region does not have a major area of production to influence global supply and demand, such as Brent in Europe or West Texas Intermediate in the United States.
However, NYMEX has discounted the possibility of a basket of crudes based on sour grades because of the failure of a Dubai futures contract on SIMEX.

The only crude futures contract listed in Asia is Brent, which trades during Singapore hours on a mutual offset basis against Brent traded in London on the International Petroleum Exchange (IPE). Traders who open positions in Singapore can
close them during London trading.
But the IPE, SIMEX and NYMEX plan to hold talks on listing Brent alongside the NYMEX crude contract on an screen based system most probably ACCESS.
SIMEX is planning to launch a revised fuel oil futures contract on April 22, with more attractive terms for traders.
The original contract was launched in 1989 but has been dormant, but still listed, since August 1995.
-- Singapore Newsroom (65-870-3082)
